title: The bean field
hook: he hoed beans to know beans, and to learn patience (Walden 7)

segments.voice: Yesterday, three chairs: one for solitude, two for friendship, three for society. Your line was three chairs. Who ended up in your second chair? Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

Early morning, a field near a pond, and a man with a hoe. The rows are long, the weeds are quick, and something keeps nibbling the young leaves overnight. He works through the dew, row after row, until the sun gets high. Then he goes in. Tomorrow, the same. A neighbor passing on the road might see nothing but a man doing a farmer's job, and not a very efficient one. Thoreau saw something else. He gave this field a whole chapter of Walden, called The Bean-Field, and in it he says he was determined to know beans.
screen: `A MAN WITH A HOE.` → `ROW AFTER ROW.` → `DETERMINED TO KNOW BEANS.`

segments.voice: First, the work itself. Thoreau describes his daily labor as making the earth "say beans instead of grass." It's a funny line, and an honest one. The ground wanted to grow its own things. He was asking it, every morning, to grow his. Second, the question he can't quite answer. He asks himself why he should raise beans at all, and he doesn't give a tidy reason. He grew to love his rows, he says, though there were more of them than he needed. The love came from the doing, not from a plan. Third, the joke inside the title. In plain American speech, someone who doesn't know beans doesn't know much. Thoreau turns the phrase around. He spent a summer bent over one plant, and he means it: he wanted to know beans, really know them, the way you only know something you've tended with your own hands. Elsewhere in the chapter he says some people must work in fields so that a parable-maker will one day have words to use. He was farming and writing the parable at the same time. Fourth, the patience. Beans don't hurry. And the field is never only yours. Thoreau names his enemies plainly: "worms, cool days, and most of all woodchucks." But by the end of the chapter he softens. He wonders whether the beans grow partly for the woodchucks, and he writes, "These beans have results which are not harvested by me." The patience he learned wasn't just waiting. It was letting the field belong to more than him.
screen: `SAY BEANS INSTEAD OF GRASS.` · `WHY RAISE THEM AT ALL?` · `DETERMINED TO KNOW BEANS.` · then, large: `THE WOODCHUCKS' SHARE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tend one plant. If there's a plant near you, a houseplant, a weed in a crack, a tree outside the window, turn toward it. If not, bring to mind one you've known. Settle and breathe. Look at it the way a person looks at something they mean to know. One leaf. Its edge. Where it's growing toward. Notice that it's in no hurry at all. If you can, give it one small thing: a little water, a dead leaf removed, a bit of light. Then let it be. The bell holds the time.
The bean field. Thoreau's long rows at Walden, where he set out to know beans and found that the harvest was never only his. Today's word.

Your line: to know beans. That closes this week of Walden, from simplify to the bean rows. Today, give one living thing a few slow minutes of care, and let it grow at its own speed. Day one thousand two hundred thirty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Walden often take the bean field as a picture of slow, attentive work: tending something by hand until you know it, and accepting that what you grow is shared with more than you.
